question: Before approving a resident producer license, the commissioner must find that the applicant is at least:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-32(a)(1) requires a resident applicant to be at least 18. The applicant must also complete prelicensing education, pass the exam and pay the fees.

question: Before taking the state exam for the life authority, an applicant must complete an approved prelicensing course of at least:
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:17-3.4(c) sets 20 hours of prelicensing education for each of the life, health, property, casualty, title and personal lines authorities. Twenty-four hours is the continuing education requirement per license term.

question: An applicant for the life authority holds the CLU designation. Under current New Jersey rules, the designation:
optionA: Waives the course, not the exam
optionB: Waives both the course and exam
optionC: Waives the exam, not the course
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:17-3.4(g) lets the Department waive prelicensing education for listed designations, but the PSI candidate bulletin states that designation holders are no longer exempt from the exam. The waiver letter expires in 90 days unless renewed for good cause.

question: A candidate passes the New Jersey producer exam. The PSI passing score report is valid for:
explanation: The PSI New Jersey Candidate Information Bulletin states that score reports are valid for one year only. A candidate who waits longer must retest before applying.

question: A candidate passes the exam and qualifies for a temporary work authority. Working under a licensed producer's supervision, she may transact business for:
explanation: The PSI bulletin states the temporary work authority lasts 60 days from the exam date under a licensed producer's supervision, and N.J.A.C. 11:17-2.5(a) caps it at 60 days. The 180-day figure is the temporary license after a producer's death or disability.

question: After the first license term, a New Jersey individual producer license expires:
optionD: Every 2 years, end of birth month
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:17-2.1(a) sets the first term to end on the last day of the birth month at least 18 months after issue, then every two years on the last day of the birth month. Business entity licenses follow a separate schedule.

question: An individual producer lets the license lapse for nonpayment. It may be reinstated without retaking the exam if the producer acts within:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-33(c) allows reinstatement within 12 months of the renewal fee due date without an exam, with a penalty of up to double the unpaid fee. N.J.A.C. 11:17-2.6(c) also requires proof of CE and a statement of any business written while unlicensed.

question: To renew, a resident producer with life, health, property or casualty authority must complete how much CE each license term?
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:17-3.6(a) requires 24 credit hours of approved CE per licensing term, including three hours on professional ethics; one ethics hour may be replaced by an insurance fraud hour. Prelicensing courses do not count.

question: A producer completes more than the 24 required CE credits in one license term. Under N.J.A.C. 11:17-3.6, the producer may:
optionB: Carry up to 24 credits over once
explanation: Excess credits up to 12 may be carried over to the next renewal term, only once, and ethics credits may not be carried over. Extra hours beyond 12 are simply lost.

question: When an insurer signs an agency contract with a licensed producer, it must file notice of the appointment with the Department within:
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:17-2.10(a)2 requires the insurer to file the notice within 15 days after the contract is executed or the producer's first application is submitted. N.J.S.A. 17:22A-42(b) likewise requires notice of a cancellation within 15 days.

question: Producer A employs licensed Producer B under a written employment contract, and B commits misconduct with a client. Producer A:
optionC: Is liable only if A signed the policy
optionD: Is responsible only for unlicensed staff
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:17-2.10(b)4 makes an employing producer responsible for the insurance-related conduct of an employed producer, and the employment contract is prima facie evidence that the employer knew. Independent contractors, by contrast, are not responsible for each other without knowledge.

question: A producer dies, and his spouse needs time to sell the agency. Without an exam, the commissioner may issue her a temporary license for no more than:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-37 and N.J.A.C. 11:17-2.11 allow a temporary license of up to 180 days for a surviving spouse or representative, with a licensed sponsor. Sixty days is the limit for a new licensee's temporary work authority.

question: A producer licensed in Pennsylvania moves to New Jersey. To become a resident licensee without new prelicensing education or exam, she must apply within:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-35(b) requires an application within 90 days of establishing legal residence, with no prelicensing education or exam for lines already held. N.J.A.C. 11:17-2.5(b) separately requires notice of the new address within 30 days.

question: A person whose New Jersey producer license was revoked may apply for reinstatement no sooner than:
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:17D-2.7(a) allows an application for reinstatement after five years from the effective date of the revocation order. The applicant must file an affidavit about activities since revocation and meet the professional qualification rules.

question: An applicant says an existing life policy may be replaced. No later than when the application is taken, the producer must:
optionD: Present and offer to read the notice
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-2.3(b) requires the producer to present and offer to read the replacement notice, signed by both, listing each policy to be replaced. The replacing insurer then notifies the existing insurer within five business days.

question: A producer moves her business office to a new address. She must notify the Department of the change within:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-33(f) and N.J.A.C. 11:17-2.8(f)2 require notice of any change of business, residence or email address within 30 days, and proof of the notice must be kept for five years.

question: A producer is disciplined by another state's insurance regulator. She must report it to the New Jersey commissioner within 30 days of:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-47(a) requires a report of any administrative action in another jurisdiction within 30 days of its final disposition, with a copy of the order. Failing to report can lead to a temporary suspension under N.J.S.A. 17:22A-47.1.

question: Before a resident producer does business under a name other than her legal name, she must:
optionA: Register it with the county clerk only
optionC: Have the name approved by DOBI
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-36 requires notice to the commissioner before an assumed name is used, and N.J.A.C. 11:17-2.8(a) bars using it until the Department files and approves it. Filing with the county clerk alone is not enough.

question: Under N.J.A.C. 11:17-2.9, a registered branch office may engage in insurance-related conduct only when:
optionA: Its manager holds a law degree
optionB: It is open 40 hours a week
optionC: The main office approves in writing
explanation: A branch office may not engage in insurance-related conduct unless at least one licensed individual producer is present, though it may stay open to service accounts during a brief absence. Branch registrations expire with the producer's license.

question: Unless a contract, statute or residual market rule provides otherwise, a producer must remit premium funds to the insurer within:
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:17C-2.2(a) requires premiums to be remitted within five business days after receipt. Premiums are held as a fiduciary and may not be commingled with the producer's own funds under N.J.A.C. 11:17C-2.1.

question: A producer must keep a designated trust account for premiums if she holds them more than five business days or if she:
optionB: Deposits them in a bank account
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:17C-2.3(a) requires a trust account when premiums are held over five business days, or when collected premiums are deposited in any account or otherwise used even if remitted on time. The account must be labeled Trust Account.

question: A producer receives a policy from the insurer to deliver to the insured. Unless the insured agrees in writing to a longer period, it must be delivered within:
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:17A-4.6 requires policies and other evidence of insurance received for delivery to be delivered or mailed within 10 calendar days of receipt. Only title policies prepared by the producer have a 30-day rule.

question: The Department writes to a producer about a consumer complaint but gives no deadline. The producer must reply in writing within:
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:17A-4.8 requires a written reply within the time the inquiry sets, or within 15 calendar days of the date it was made or mailed when no time is given.

question: Which free offering may a producer give health and life clients without violating New Jersey's rebating rules?
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:17A-2.3(g) permits free services that relate to or enhance the insurance, such as gym or wellness discounts with life and health products. Cash or event tickets worth more than $100 are prohibited inducements under 11:17A-2.3(h).

question: A producer offers to donate to a qualified charity whenever a client buys a policy. Under N.J.A.C. 11:17A-2.3(f), one condition for this to be allowed is that:
optionA: The client takes the tax deduction
optionC: The donation is paid to the client
explanation: A charitable contribution is not a rebate if the producer gets no benefit beyond the tax deduction, no tax benefit passes to the consumer, the premium and commission are not altered, and records are kept five years.

question: A producer completes an application in a face-to-face meeting and the applicant signs it. Unless the insurer waived it in writing, the producer must:
optionB: Mail the form to the applicant
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:17A-4.2 requires the producer to witness the applicant's signature before submitting an application signed after a face-to-face meeting. The insurer may waive this in writing in advance.

question: A producer comes to believe a claimant submitted a false claim. Under N.J.S.A. 17:33A-9, the producer must notify the state's fraud authorities:
optionC: Only if the claim is paid
explanation: Anyone who believes a violation of the Insurance Fraud Prevention Act has occurred must notify the Department's Bureau of Fraud Deterrence and the Office of the Insurance Fraud Prosecutor immediately after discovery. Good-faith reporters are immune from civil liability under 17:33A-9(b).

question: An applicant knowingly gives false material information on an application to obtain a policy. Under N.J.S.A. 17:33A-4, this is:
optionA: A violation of the Fraud Act
optionB: Fraud only if a claim is filed
optionC: A matter for the insurer alone
optionD: Allowed if corrected in two years
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:33A-4(a)(4)(b) makes it a violation to prepare a statement for an insurer or producer to obtain a policy knowing it contains false material information. No claim needs to be filed.

question: Under the Insurance Fraud Prevention Act, the civil penalty for a third or later violation may be as much as:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:33A-5 sets penalties of up to $5,000 for the first violation, $10,000 for the second and $15,000 for each later violation, plus court costs and attorneys' fees. The commissioner may also refer the matter for criminal prosecution or licensing action.

question: Under New Jersey law, a producer may use the existence of the Life and Health Insurance Guaranty Association in a sales presentation:
optionC: Never, as an inducement to buy
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:32A-17(a) bars any insurer, agent or producer from using the association's existence for sales, solicitation or inducement to purchase. Insurers instead deliver an approved summary document with its disclaimer.

question: A life insurer must belong to the New Jersey Life and Health Insurance Guaranty Association:
optionA: Only if it elects to join the plan
optionB: Only if rated below an A
optionC: Only if domiciled in New Jersey
optionD: As a condition of its authority
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:32A-5(a) makes membership a condition of a member insurer's authority to do business in New Jersey, and a member remains one for four years after its certificate ends. The association keeps separate life and annuity and health accounts.

question: Under New Jersey law, the Commissioner of Banking and Insurance is appointed by:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:1-2 provides that the commissioner is appointed by the Governor with the advice and consent of the Senate and serves at the Governor's pleasure. The NAIC drafts model laws but appoints no state regulator.

question: In addition to its other powers, N.J.S.A. 17:1-15 lets the commissioner deal with a person violating Title 17 or 17B by:
optionA: Ordering it to cease and desist
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:1-15(j) gives the commissioner power to order any person violating Title 17 or Title 17B to cease and desist. Contempt punishment comes from a court, which the commissioner may ask to enforce a subpoena.

question: To protect the public, the commissioner enters an immediate order on ex parte proofs during a producer licensing case. A preliminary hearing must be held within:
explanation: Under N.J.S.A. 17:22A-45(d), an ex parte order may be challenged on 10 days' notice, and a preliminary hearing must be held in any event within 20 days after it is entered. The 10 days is the notice period for a motion to vacate, not the hearing deadline.

question: Under N.J.S.A. 17:22A-45, the general civil penalty for a person's first violation of the Producer Licensing Act may not exceed:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-45(c) sets a penalty of up to $5,000 for the first offense and up to $10,000 for each later offense, plus restitution and the costs of investigation. $10,000 is the cap for repeat offenses.

question: Which 1869 Supreme Court decision held that issuing an insurance policy is not interstate commerce, leaving regulation to the states?
explanation: Paul v. Virginia (1869) held that an insurance policy is not a transaction of commerce, so the states regulated insurance alone for 75 years. South-Eastern Underwriters (1944) reversed that view.

question: In United States v. South-Eastern Underwriters Association (1944), the Supreme Court held that insurance:
optionD: May be regulated only by states
explanation: South-Eastern Underwriters held that insurance sold across state lines is interstate commerce subject to federal law, including the Sherman Act. Congress answered in 1945 with the McCarran-Ferguson Act (Public Law 15), returning primary regulation to the states.

question: A person who, for a fee, advises clients on the benefits and drawbacks of policies sold in New Jersey, without selling them, is acting as:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-28 defines an insurance consultant as a person who, for a fee or other consideration, offers advice on the benefits or drawbacks of policies; attorneys and CPAs paid no commission are excluded. A broker obtains coverage for buyers, which this person does not do.

question: Under the Producer Licensing Act, conferring directly with a buyer about the benefits and terms of a particular policy, by a person who sells insurance, is called:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-28 defines negotiate as conferring directly with or advising a buyer about a particular policy's substantive benefits, terms or conditions. Soliciting is attempting to sell or urging a person to apply.

question: Under N.J.S.A. 17:22A-28, a producer license by itself gives the holder:
optionA: Authority to bind any admitted insurer
optionD: No authority to commit an insurer
explanation: The Act's definition of license states that the license itself creates no actual, apparent or inherent authority to represent or commit an insurer. That authority comes from an insurer's appointment under N.J.S.A. 17:22A-42.

question: An insurer that does not hold a current New Jersey certificate of authority is, in New Jersey:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:17-11 calls an insurer authorized only if it holds a current certificate of authority from the commissioner; any other insurer is unauthorized. Foreign describes where an insurer was formed, not whether it is authorized.

question: Under the McCarran-Ferguson Act of 1945, primary responsibility for regulating the business of insurance belongs to:
explanation: McCarran-Ferguson declared that state regulation of insurance is in the public interest, so each state's insurance department and commissioner license insurers and producers and enforce the insurance code. The NAIC only drafts model laws and has no enforcement power, and federal law reaches insurance only where a federal statute specifically addresses it.

question: An insurer incorporated in Bermuda wants to sell life insurance policies to residents of New Jersey. In New Jersey, this company is classified as:
explanation: Under N.J.S.A. 17B:17-7, an alien insurer is formed under the laws of a country other than the United States. A foreign insurer is formed in a different U.S. state, which is the tempting choice but applies only to companies formed within the United States.

question: An insurer incorporated in Ohio has received a certificate of authority from New Jersey and sells policies there. In New Jersey, it is considered:
explanation: Under N.J.S.A. 17B:17-7 and 17B:17-11, a company formed in another state is foreign, and one holding a current certificate of authority is admitted (authorized). Non-admitted would apply only if it lacked a certificate, and it is domestic only in Ohio.

question: Maria shops her client's needs among many insurers and, when placing the business, legally represents the client rather than any insurer. Maria is acting as:
explanation: A broker represents the insured or applicant, while an agent, whether captive or independent, represents the insurers that appointed him. An independent agent can also place business with many insurers, but he still legally represents those insurers, not the client.

question: An insurer declines a life insurance applicant based partly on information in a consumer report. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, the insurer must:
optionA: Tell the applicant and name the reporting agency
optionB: Keep the consumer report secret from the applicant
optionD: Get approval from the state commissioner before declining
explanation: When adverse action is based on a consumer report, the FCRA requires the insurer to notify the applicant and identify the reporting agency so the person can get a free copy and dispute inaccurate information. The commissioner does not approve individual underwriting decisions.

question: Which statement about federal privacy and telemarketing rules affecting insurance producers is accurate?
optionA: Do Not Call rules exempt all insurance telemarketing calls
optionB: GLBA bans insurers from sharing any customer data
optionC: Insurers must provide customers privacy notices
optionD: Registry numbers may be called once per calendar year
explanation: The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act requires insurers to give privacy notices explaining their information-sharing practices and to let consumers opt out of sharing nonpublic personal information with nonaffiliated third parties. Insurance telemarketers must honor the National Do Not Call Registry, subject to limited exceptions such as an established business relationship.

question: An insurer can predict expected losses more accurately as the number of similar exposure units it insures grows larger. This principle is called:
explanation: The law of large numbers holds that the larger the group of similar exposure units, the more closely actual losses will match predicted losses. Adverse selection is the tendency of poorer risks to seek coverage, which works against predictability rather than describing it.

question: An insurer notices that people in poor health are more likely to apply for life insurance than healthy people. This tendency is called:
explanation: Adverse selection is the tendency of poorer-than-average risks to seek insurance more often, which insurers control through underwriting. Moral hazard refers to an applicant's dishonesty, not the tendency of high-risk people to buy coverage.

question: A person who has been declared legally insane by a court signs an application for life insurance. Which element of a valid contract is missing?
explanation: A contract requires competent parties, meaning people of legal age and sound mind who are not under the influence of drugs or alcohol. Consideration is the premium and application statements exchanged for the insurer's promise, which is not the problem here.

question: Dana pays her first $400 premium and dies in an accident a week later, and her beneficiary receives $250,000. This illustrates that the policy is:
explanation: An aleatory contract involves an unequal exchange of values that depends on an uncertain event, so a small premium can buy a large benefit. Unilateral means only the insurer makes an enforceable promise, which is true but is not what the unequal exchange shows.

question: The insurer is legally bound to pay covered claims, but the insured cannot be sued for choosing to stop paying premiums. This makes the policy:
explanation: In a unilateral contract only the insurer makes a legally enforceable promise; the insured may stop paying and the policy simply lapses. Conditional means the insurer pays only if the insured meets conditions such as paying premiums and submitting proof of loss.

question: A policy provision is ambiguous, and a court interprets it in favor of the insured because the insurer wrote the contract. This reflects that the policy is a contract of:
explanation: Insurance is a contract of adhesion, offered on a take-it-or-leave-it basis with wording written by the insurer, so any ambiguity is construed against the insurer. Utmost good faith refers to the honesty both parties owe each other, not to how unclear wording is read.

question: Which characteristic of insurance contracts means each party relies on the other's honesty, with no attempt to conceal or deceive?
explanation: Utmost good faith means the insurer and applicant are each entitled to rely on the other's statements, which is why concealment or material misrepresentation can void coverage. A personal contract refers to coverage of a specific individual whose character matters to the insurer, not to the duty of honesty.

question: Statements an applicant makes on a life insurance application are considered true to the best of the applicant's knowledge and belief. These statements are:
explanation: Application answers are representations, true to the best of the applicant's belief, and only a material misrepresentation lets the insurer void the contract. Warranties are statements guaranteed to be literally true, where any breach could void the contract, which is why application answers are not treated as warranties.

question: An applicant knows she had a heart attack last year but intentionally withholds that fact from the insurer to obtain coverage. This is:
explanation: Concealment is intentionally withholding a known material fact, and it can void the policy within the contestable period. Misrepresentation is making a false statement, and fraud is an intentional deception meant to induce the other party to act to its harm.

question: For two years an insurer accepted late premiums without objection. When it later tries to lapse the policy over a late payment, a court prevents it. This is:
explanation: Estoppel prevents a party from reasserting a right it has given up when the other party relied on that conduct. Waiver is the voluntary giving up of a known right, which is what the insurer did by accepting late premiums; estoppel is the legal bar that results.

question: An applicant pays the first premium with the application and gets a conditional receipt. She dies after the medical exam but before policy issue, and she was insurable. The insurer:
optionD: Denies the claim since no policy issued
explanation: Under a conditional receipt, coverage begins on the later of the application or medical exam date if the applicant proves insurable as applied for, so the claim is paid. A binding receipt, by contrast, gives temporary coverage immediately for a limited period whether or not the applicant is later found insurable.

question: An applicant paid no premium with the application. When the producer delivers the issued policy, the producer should collect the premium and:
optionA: Have the applicant retake the medical exam
optionB: Backdate the policy to the application date
optionC: Obtain a signed statement of good health
explanation: When no premium was paid with the application, the producer collects it at delivery along with a statement of good health confirming the applicant's health has not changed since applying. A new medical exam is not routinely required, and the application attached to the policy becomes part of the entire contract.

question: No premium was paid with an application. The policy is issued on May 1 and delivered on May 10, when the producer collects the premium. Coverage begins:
explanation: With no premium at application, coverage starts only when the policy is delivered, the first premium is paid and a statement of good health is signed, which all happened on May 10. Issuing the policy on May 1 does not start coverage because the insurer had not yet received the premium.

question: Maria bought a policy on her husband's life, then they divorced. He dies five years later while she still owns the policy. The insurer will:
optionA: Pay Maria, since insurable interest existed at application
optionB: Deny the claim because insurable interest ended at the divorce
optionC: Refund premiums only, since the marriage had ended
optionD: Pay his estate instead of the named beneficiary
explanation: For life insurance, insurable interest must exist only when the policy is applied for, not at the time of death. The divorce does not void the policy, so denying the claim for lack of insurable interest at death is wrong.

question: Which of the following would NOT typically have an insurable interest in the life of the proposed insured?
optionA: A business relying on the insured as a key employee
optionB: A creditor, up to the amount of the debt
optionC: The insured's spouse of ten years
optionD: A neighbor who has known the insured for years
explanation: Insurable interest requires a financial stake or close family tie in the insured's continued life; friendship alone does not qualify. A creditor does have an insurable interest, but only up to the amount owed.

question: Ellen applies for and owns a policy on her husband's life, with his consent, and names herself beneficiary. Which statement about this arrangement is true?
optionA: It is third-party ownership, and Ellen controls the policy
optionB: Her husband must own the policy because he is the insured person
optionC: The policy is void unless he is the owner
optionD: Ellen cannot be both the owner and the beneficiary
explanation: When the owner and the insured are different people, the policy is third-party owned and the owner holds all policy rights, provided the insured consents. Nothing bars an owner with insurable interest from also being the beneficiary.

question: In group life insurance, who is the policyowner, and what do the covered employees receive?
optionA: Each employee owns an individual policy; the employer gets certificates
optionB: The insurer owns the policy; employees get riders
optionC: The employer owns a master policy; employees get certificates
optionD: The union owns the policy; employees get individual contracts
explanation: The employer is the policyowner of a single master contract, and each insured employee receives a certificate of insurance describing the coverage. Individual ownership by each employee is how individual, not group, insurance works.

question: Raj leaves his job, where he had $100,000 of group term life. He has since developed heart disease. To keep coverage, he should:
optionA: Apply for new individual term with a medical exam
optionB: Continue the group life coverage for 18 months under COBRA
optionC: Convert to an individual permanent policy within 31 days
optionD: Convert within 90 days with evidence of insurability
explanation: New Jersey requires every group life policy to let a person whose coverage ends with employment convert to an individual policy, without evidence of insurability, if he applies and pays within 31 days (N.J.S.A. 17B:27-72(i)). COBRA continuation applies to group health plans, not group life.

question: An insured with a terminal diagnosis wants cash for treatment without selling his policy. Which feature lets the insurer pay part of the death benefit early?
optionD: A viatical settlement contract with a provider
explanation: Accelerated (living) benefits let the insurer advance part of the death benefit to a terminally ill insured, and the amount paid reduces what the beneficiary later receives. A viatical settlement also provides cash but requires selling the policy to a third party.

question: A widow, 38, has a son who just turned 16. Her own Social Security survivor benefits stop until she reaches age 60. This gap is called the:
explanation: A surviving parent's benefits end when the youngest child turns 16 and do not resume until the survivor reaches 60, a gap called the blackout period. An elimination period is the waiting time before disability income benefits begin.

question: Kevin and Lisa have a 30-year, $300,000 mortgage and want coverage that shrinks as the loan balance falls. Which policy fits best?
explanation: Decreasing term has a level premium and a face amount that declines over the term, roughly matching a mortgage balance. Level term would keep paying the full $300,000 even after much of the loan is repaid, costing more than needed.

question: Tom bought 20-year convertible term at age 30. At 45 he is diagnosed with diabetes and wants lifelong coverage. What can he do?
optionA: Convert to whole life without evidence of insurability
optionB: Renew the term for another 20 years at the original rate
optionC: Apply for whole life with a new medical exam
optionD: Add an increasing term rider to extend the coverage
explanation: The conversion privilege lets Tom exchange term for permanent insurance without proving insurability, usually at his attained age. Applying with a new exam would expose him to a rating or decline because of the diabetes.

question: Dr. Chen, 40, wants permanent coverage but wants no premiums due after she retires at 65. Which policy fits?
explanation: Limited pay whole life compresses premiums into a set period, such as to age 65, after which the policy is paid up for life. Straight whole life requires premiums for the insured's entire life.

question: A self-employed contractor with uneven income wants permanent coverage and the ability to skip or reduce premiums in lean years. Which policy fits best?
explanation: Universal life has flexible premiums: the owner can pay more, less or skip a payment as long as the cash value covers the monthly charges. Variable life has fixed, scheduled premiums.

question: A client wants permanent coverage with fixed premiums, accepts market risk, and wants the cash value invested in stock subaccounts. Which policy fits?
explanation: Variable life invests cash value in separate account subaccounts chosen by the owner, with a fixed premium and the owner bearing investment risk. Indexed universal life only credits interest linked to an index and does not invest directly in stocks.

question: A wealthy married couple wants a policy to pay the estate taxes due after the second spouse dies. Which policy fits best?
explanation: Survivorship life pays only at the second death, when estate taxes usually come due because of the unlimited marital deduction at the first death, and it costs less than two single policies. Joint first-to-die life pays too early, at the first death.

question: A New Jersey individual life policy must let the owner cancel it for a full refund of premiums and fees within at least:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-2.1 requires every individual life policy to allow cancellation and a prompt refund for at least 10 days after the policyholder receives it. A replacement policy carries a longer 30-day right under N.J.A.C. 11:4-2.4.

question: A New Jersey life policy lapsed for nonpayment and was not surrendered for cash. The owner may apply to reinstate it within:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-9 requires a reinstatement right for 3 years from the first unpaid premium, with evidence of insurability and back premiums plus interest, unless the cash value is exhausted or extended term has expired. Thirty-one days is a typical grace or conversion period, not the reinstatement window.

question: A life policy delivered in New Jersey may not limit the time for suing the insurer to less than:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-15 prohibits any life policy provision limiting the time to bring an action to less than five years after the cause of action accrues. Three years is the familiar health policy outer limit.

question: When a new life policy replaces existing coverage, the replacing insurer must give the owner the right to return it for a full refund within:
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-2.4(a)5 requires the replacing insurer to give notice of a 30-day right to return the policy for an unconditional full refund. The ordinary individual life free look is 10 days.

question: Months after issue, an insurer wants to rely on a statement the applicant made in a separate letter that was never attached to the policy. Under the entire contract provision:
optionA: The letter may be used during the contestable period
optionB: The letter becomes part of the policy automatically
optionC: The letter cannot be used against the insured
optionD: The letter controls if it conflicts with the policy
explanation: The entire contract provision says the policy plus the attached application is the whole agreement, so unattached statements cannot be used. Timing within the contestable period does not change that; only attached documents count.

question: Which part of a life insurance policy contains the insurer's basic promise to pay the death benefit to the beneficiary?
explanation: The insuring clause is the insurer's promise to pay and usually appears on the policy face. The consideration clause instead covers what the applicant gives in exchange: the application and the premium.

question: Maria owns and pays for a life policy on her adult son, who is the insured. Who may change the beneficiary or take a policy loan?
explanation: Ownership rights such as naming beneficiaries, borrowing and assigning belong to the policyowner, not the insured. The insured's consent is needed at application, but not to exercise later ownership rights.

question: A $100,000 policy has a $1,200 annual premium due March 1 that goes unpaid. The insured dies March 20. The insurer will pay:
explanation: New Jersey requires a grace period of 30 days, or one month of at least 30 days (N.J.S.A. 17B:25-3), so the policy was still in force on March 20. The insurer pays the face amount minus the overdue premium: $100,000 - $1,200 = $98,800, not the full $100,000.

question: A policyowner misses a premium and the grace period ends. Her whole life policy has enough cash value and an automatic premium loan provision. What happens?
optionA: The premium is borrowed from the cash value
optionB: The policy converts to extended term
optionC: The policy lapses and must be reinstated
optionD: The policy becomes reduced paid-up insurance
explanation: The automatic premium loan provision pays the overdue premium as a loan against the cash value, keeping the policy in force. Extended term would apply only if there were no APL provision and no option chosen.

question: Three years after issue, an insured dies, and the insurer discovers he concealed a heart condition on the application. Premiums were paid. The insurer:
optionB: May deny the claim for concealment
optionC: May refund premiums instead of paying
optionD: May reduce the benefit by half
explanation: After the two-year incontestable period, the insurer cannot contest for misrepresentation or concealment. The exceptions are nonpayment of premium and, in some cases, impersonation or lack of insurable interest, none of which applies here.

question: An insured dies with a $100,000 policy. He paid $20 per $1,000, but the correct premium for his true age was $25 per $1,000. The insurer pays:
explanation: Under misstatement of age, the benefit is adjusted to what the premium paid would have bought: $2,000 paid / $25 per $1,000 = 80 units, or $80,000. The contract is not voided, and the full face is not paid.

question: A policy excludes war, private piloting and suicide within two years. Which death, occurring three years after issue, is covered?
optionC: Crash while piloting a private plane
explanation: The suicide clause applies only during the first two years (during which premiums are refunded), so a suicide in year three is covered. War and private aviation exclusions remain in effect for the life of the policy.

question: To secure a bank loan, a business owner temporarily transfers part of his policy's rights to the bank, which is repaid first at death. This is:
explanation: A collateral assignment is temporary and partial: the lender is repaid from proceeds and the rest goes to the beneficiary. An absolute assignment permanently transfers all ownership rights.

question: Tom names his wife primary beneficiary and his two children contingent beneficiaries. His wife dies first, and Tom later dies without changing anything. Proceeds go to:
explanation: Contingent beneficiaries receive the proceeds when no primary beneficiary survives the insured. Proceeds go to the estate only if no named beneficiary survives, so probate is not involved.

question: As part of a divorce settlement, Ken named his ex-wife the irrevocable beneficiary. He now wants to name his new wife instead. He:
optionA: May change it by notifying the insurer
optionD: Must wait for the next policy anniversary
explanation: An irrevocable beneficiary has a vested interest, so the owner cannot change the designation without that beneficiary's consent. Notice alone works only for a revocable beneficiary.

question: An insured and his primary beneficiary die in the same car crash, and no one can tell who died first. Under the Uniform Simultaneous Death Act, proceeds are paid:
optionA: As if the beneficiary survived the insured
optionB: As if the insured survived the beneficiary
optionC: Equally to the estates of the insured and beneficiary
explanation: The Uniform Simultaneous Death Act presumes the insured survived, so proceeds go to the contingent beneficiary or the insured's estate. A common disaster clause adds a short survival period requirement for the same purpose.

question: A father names his 8-year-old daughter as beneficiary but sets up no trust or guardian, then dies. The insurer will most likely:
optionA: Pay the proceeds directly to the child
optionB: Pay a court-appointed guardian for her
optionC: Pay the proceeds to the father's estate
optionD: Hold the proceeds until she turns 25
explanation: Minors cannot legally receive and manage proceeds, so the insurer pays a court-appointed guardian or a trust. Naming a trust or guardian in advance avoids court delays.

question: A policyowner stops paying premiums on a whole life policy with cash value, has no automatic premium loan, and never chooses a nonforfeiture option. The insurer applies:
explanation: Extended term is the automatic option in most policies: the cash value buys term coverage for the same face amount for as long as it lasts. Reduced paid-up must be elected.

question: A policyowner wants each year's dividends to buy additional permanent coverage with no evidence of insurability. Which dividend option should she choose?
explanation: Paid-up additions use dividends as single premiums for small amounts of paid-up permanent insurance with no underwriting. One-year term buys temporary coverage, not permanent.

question: A beneficiary wants $2,000 a month for as long as the proceeds and interest last. Which settlement option does this describe?
explanation: Fixed amount sets the payment size, and the length depends on how long the money lasts. Fixed period sets the length instead and lets the payment size vary.

question: An insured with a waiver of premium rider becomes totally disabled. When does the insurer usually begin waiving premiums?
optionA: After a waiting period, typically six months
optionB: On the first day the insured becomes disabled
explanation: Waiver of premium typically requires a waiting period of about six months of total disability, often refunding premiums paid during it. Waiver from day one is not standard.

question: A 28-year-old wants the right to buy more coverage at set ages and at marriage or a child's birth without proving insurability. He needs a:
explanation: The guaranteed insurability option lets the insured buy set amounts at specified ages or events with no evidence of insurability. A cost of living rider only adjusts coverage for inflation.

question: During which phase of a deferred annuity does the owner pay premiums while the account earns tax-deferred interest?
explanation: Premiums are paid and earnings build tax-deferred during the accumulation phase. The annuitization (payout) phase comes later, when the value is converted into a stream of income.

question: A 66-year-old retiree deposits a $200,000 lump sum and wants income to start next month. Which annuity best fits her goal?
explanation: An immediate annuity is bought with a single premium and begins payments within 12 months. A single premium deferred annuity is funded the same way but postpones income for years, which does not meet her need.

question: A policyowner pays a large single premium, and the policy fails the 7-pay test. Which consequence follows?
optionA: The death benefit becomes taxable income
optionB: Loans and withdrawals are taxed LIFO, possibly with penalty
optionC: The policy can regain non-MEC status after seven years
optionD: The cash value stops growing tax-deferred
explanation: A policy failing the 7-pay test becomes a modified endowment contract: loans and withdrawals are taxed earnings-first, with a 10% penalty before 59 1/2, while a non-MEC loan is not taxable. The death benefit stays income tax-free, and once a MEC, always a MEC.

question: A 35-year-old expects to be in a higher tax bracket in retirement and wants tax-free income then. Which account best fits?
explanation: Roth IRA contributions are made after tax, and qualified withdrawals are entirely tax-free, which helps most when future rates are higher; the owner also has no RMDs. A traditional IRA gives a deduction now but taxes withdrawals later at the higher rate.

question: Before selling an annuity in New Jersey, the producer must make reasonable efforts to obtain and record the consumer's:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-38(b) requires reasonable grounds to believe an annuity is suitable, based on information about the consumer's financial status, tax status and investment objectives recorded on the commissioner's form.

question: A producer selling annuities uses a self-conferred senior specialist title in her ads. Under N.J.S.A. 17B:25-36, this is:
optionB: A misleading use of a designation
explanation: The statute treats a nonexistent or self-conferred certification or designation implying special expertise with seniors as untrue, deceptive or misleading in annuity sales. Accredited designations earned through real standards are presumed proper.

question: A carpenter wants a policy that replaces part of his paycheck if an injury or illness keeps him from working. He needs:
explanation: Disability income insurance replaces a portion of earnings lost to accident or sickness. Major medical pays medical bills, not lost income.

question: An HMO member wants to see a dermatologist for a skin condition. Under a typical HMO, the member must first:
optionA: Pay the full cost, then file a claim
optionC: Choose any dermatologist, in or out of the network
optionD: Get a referral from her primary care physician
explanation: The HMO primary care physician acts as a gatekeeper, and specialist visits require a referral. HMOs usually charge copays rather than requiring members to pay in full and file claims.

question: A PPO member sees an out-of-network specialist without any referral. How will the plan typically treat the claim?
optionB: It pays benefits, but at a lower level
optionC: It pays the same as in-network care
optionD: It requires a PCP referral before paying
explanation: PPOs allow out-of-network care without referrals, but the member pays more through higher deductibles and coinsurance. Denying out-of-network care except emergencies is typical of an HMO or EPO, not a PPO.

question: Which plan type lets members decide at each visit between gatekeeper network care and out-of-network care at higher cost?
explanation: A point-of-service plan blends HMO and PPO features: members use a primary care gatekeeper in network but may go out of network for lower benefits. An EPO generally does not cover out-of-network care at all.

question: An applicant for an individual disability income policy wants to lower the premium. Which change would do that?
explanation: A longer elimination period works like a higher deductible in time, so the premium drops. A longer benefit period, added riders and a broader own-occupation definition all increase the premium.

question: An applicant with diabetes applies for an ACA-compliant individual major medical plan during open enrollment. The insurer may:
optionA: Not decline her or exclude the condition
optionB: Decline her for the preexisting condition
optionC: Exclude diabetes for the first 12 months
optionD: Charge her more because of her health
explanation: ACA major medical plans are guaranteed issue with no preexisting condition exclusions, and premiums may vary only by age, tobacco use, location and family size. Health-based rating is not permitted.

question: An applicant with a heart condition applies for individual disability income insurance. Unlike ACA major medical, the insurer may:
optionA: Not consider her medical history at all
optionB: Consider only age, tobacco use, location and family size
optionC: Rate, exclude the condition, or decline coverage
optionD: Issue coverage only during open enrollment
explanation: Guaranteed issue applies to ACA major medical, but disability income and long-term care are still medically underwritten. The insurer may charge more, exclude the condition with a rider, or decline the risk.

question: Which renewability provision gives the insured the greatest protection against cancellation and premium increases?
explanation: Under a noncancelable policy the insurer can neither cancel nor raise premiums, as long as premiums are paid. Guaranteed renewable also prevents cancellation but allows class-wide premium increases.

question: An insurer raises premiums for an entire class of disability policyholders, but it cannot cancel any individual policy. These policies are:
explanation: Guaranteed renewable policies must be renewed, but premiums can rise for an entire class. A noncancelable policy would not allow any premium increase.

question: A disability policy lets the insurer decline renewal only if the insured retires or leaves employment, never for health. It is:
explanation: A conditionally renewable policy lets the insurer refuse renewal only for conditions stated in the contract, such as employment status, but not deteriorating health. Optionally renewable lets the insurer refuse for any reason on a premium date.

question: To make tax-deductible contributions to a health savings account, an individual must:
optionA: Spend the full balance by year-end
optionB: Be enrolled in Medicare Part B
optionC: Be covered by a qualified high-deductible health plan
optionD: Work for an employer that sponsors and funds the account
explanation: HSA eligibility requires HDHP coverage; contributions are deductible, growth is tax-free and qualified withdrawals are tax-free. The use-it-or-lose-it rule belongs to flexible spending accounts, and HSA balances roll over.

question: A child is covered under both parents' group plans. The mother was born March 10, 1985; the father July 2, 1980. Which plan is primary?
optionD: The plan with the lower deductible
explanation: Under the birthday rule in coordination of benefits, the parent whose birthday falls earlier in the calendar year is primary, using month and day only. The father is older, but birth year does not matter.

question: An insurer pays an insured's medical bills after a crash caused by another driver, then sues that driver to recover. This right is:
explanation: Subrogation transfers the insured's right to recover from a negligent third party to the insurer that paid the claim, preventing a double recovery. Coordination of benefits applies between two health plans covering the same person.

question: A worker becomes totally disabled and qualifies for Social Security disability benefits. Benefits generally begin after a waiting period of:
explanation: Social Security disability has a 5-month waiting period. The 12-month figure is the separate requirement that the disability be expected to last at least 12 months or result in death.

question: A group health insurer learns an applicant carries a gene linked to breast cancer. Under N.J.S.A. 17B:27-36.2, the insurer may:
optionB: Not exclude or rate her for it
explanation: New Jersey bars group health policies from excluding a person or setting rates or terms based on an actual or expected health condition or any genetic characteristic. It applies to every such policy delivered, issued or renewed in New Jersey.

question: A producer sells a health insurance policy to a New Jersey resident. Under N.J.S.A. 17:22A-41.1, the producer must tell the buyer in writing:
optionA: The insurer's loss ratio for the year
optionD: The commission the producer will earn
explanation: Producers selling health insurance to New Jersey residents must disclose in writing the amount of any commission, fee or other consideration they will receive, including the percentage of premium if that is the basis.

question: Mary pays her individual health premium monthly, due June 1. She is hospitalized June 8 and has not yet paid. Her policy is:
optionA: Lapsed, because the grace period for monthly premiums is 7 days
optionB: Lapsed, because no grace period applies to health policies
optionC: In force only for accidents until the premium is paid
optionD: In force, because the grace period is 10 days
explanation: Policies with monthly premiums have a 10-day grace period, so coverage continues through June 11 and any unpaid premium can be deducted from a claim. The 7-day grace period applies only to weekly premiums, and 31 days applies to other modes.

question: Jan's lapsed health policy is reinstated on the 45th day after her conditional receipt because the insurer never responded. Coverage for a new sickness begins:
explanation: If the insurer issues a conditional receipt and does not disapprove the application, the policy is reinstated on the 45th day. After reinstatement, accidents are covered immediately but sickness only if it begins more than 10 days later, which discourages reinstating after falling ill.

question: Under the uniform provisions, the normal deadlines for notice of claim, the insurer sending claim forms, and the insured filing proof of loss are:
explanation: The insured gives notice within 20 days of the loss, the insurer must furnish claim forms within 15 days of notice, and proof of loss is due within 90 days. If forms are not sent in time, the claimant may submit proof of loss in any written form.

question: Dave's medical claim is denied and he wants to sue his insurer. Under the legal actions provision, he may file suit:
optionA: Immediately, but within 1 year of the loss
optionB: Only after 90 days and within 2 years
optionC: Only after arbitration, with no time limit
optionD: From 60 days to 3 years after proof of loss
explanation: The insured must wait 60 days after filing proof of loss, giving the insurer time to investigate, and must sue within 3 years after proof of loss was required. Suing immediately is not allowed under this provision.

question: Three years after issue, an insurer learns that an applicant made an innocent misstatement on her health application. Under the time limit on certain defenses provision, the insurer:
optionA: May rescind the policy and refund premiums
optionB: May reduce benefits to match the true facts
optionC: Cannot void it or deny claims for it
optionD: May cancel the policy with 30 days' notice
explanation: After the policy has been in force 2 years, misstatements in the application, other than fraudulent ones, cannot be used to void the policy or deny a claim. This provision works like the incontestable clause in life insurance.

question: An agent agrees in a letter to waive an exclusion on a client's individual health policy. Under the entire contract provision, the waiver is:
optionA: Valid, because the agent represents the insurer
optionB: Invalid unless an executive officer endorses it
optionC: Valid if the client signs the agent's letter
optionD: Invalid unless the state insurance department approves
explanation: The policy, endorsements and attached application form the entire contract, and only an executive officer of the insurer can approve a change, endorsed on the policy. Agents have no authority to change or waive policy provisions.

question: Which of the following is a mandatory provision under the NAIC Uniform Individual Accident and Sickness Policy Provisions Law?
explanation: The insurer may examine a claimant at its own expense while a claim is pending and request an autopsy where law allows, one of 12 mandatory provisions that also include change of beneficiary and payment of claims. Illegal occupation, intoxicants and relation of earnings are optional provisions.

question: A clerk insured under an individual disability policy becomes a commercial roofer without telling the insurer, then is injured on a roof. The insurer will:
optionA: Pay what the premium buys at the roofer's rate
optionB: Deny the claim for failure to notify it
optionC: Pay the full benefit, then raise future premiums
optionD: Rescind the policy and refund all premiums
explanation: Under the change of occupation provision, a move to a more hazardous class reduces benefits to what the premium paid would buy at the new class. A move to a less hazardous occupation instead brings a lower rate and a refund of excess premium.

question: Paul stated his age as 40, but he was 45. He pays $300 a year; the correct premium at 45 is $400. His $2,000 monthly benefit becomes:
explanation: Benefits are adjusted to what the premium paid would have bought at the correct age: $300 / $400 = 75%, and 75% x $2,000 = $1,500. The insurer neither voids the policy nor keeps paying the full benefit.

question: Mike's $2,000 health claim is approved while a $150 premium is due and unpaid. Under the unpaid premium provision, the insurer will:
optionA: Deny the claim until the premium is paid
optionC: Pay $2,000 and bill the premium separately
explanation: The unpaid premium provision lets the insurer deduct any premium due and unpaid from the claim payment: $2,000 - $150 = $1,850. The claim is not denied, because the policy is still in force.

question: Lou recovers from a back injury, returns to work for 3 months, then is disabled again by the same injury. Under a typical recurrent disability provision:
optionA: A new elimination period must be satisfied
optionB: The second disability is excluded as preexisting
optionD: Only partial disability benefits are payable
explanation: A recurrent disability from the same cause within a set time, often 6 months, is treated as a continuation of the first claim, so no new elimination period applies. A new elimination period would apply only after that time has passed or for an unrelated cause.

question: A new disability policy has a 15-day probationary period and a 30-day elimination period. The insured falls ill on day 10 of coverage. The illness is:
optionB: Covered from day 16 of coverage onward
optionC: Not covered, since it began during the probationary period
optionD: Covered immediately, since probation applies only to accidents
explanation: A probationary period applies once, at the start of coverage, and illnesses that begin during it are not covered, while accidents are covered immediately. The elimination period applies to each disability like a time deductible, but only for covered disabilities.

question: Tom's employer has 75 employees. After Tom and his wife divorce, she may continue her coverage under his group health plan through COBRA for up to:
explanation: COBRA applies to employers with 20 or more employees and allows 36 months for divorce, death of the employee, Medicare entitlement or loss of dependent status. The 18-month period applies to termination or reduced hours, extended to 29 months for a disabled beneficiary, and a conversion policy may be available within 31 days after COBRA ends.

question: A health insurer receives a complete, clean claim filed electronically. Under New Jersey's prompt pay law, it must pay the claim no later than the:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:26-9.1(d) requires payment of a clean electronic claim by the 30th calendar day after receipt, or earlier if the Medicare deadline is shorter. Paper claims get 40 days, and overdue payments bear 12 percent interest.

question: A complete, clean health claim is mailed to the insurer on paper rather than filed electronically. It must be paid no later than the:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:26-9.1(d)(1) allows 40 calendar days for claims submitted by other than electronic means, versus 30 days for electronic claims. A claim not paid on time is overdue and bears simple interest of 12 percent a year.

question: An unmarried adult child with no dependents and no other coverage may elect to stay on a parent's New Jersey group health policy until the child's:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:27-30.5 requires group policies to continue coverage on election until the dependent's 31st birthday if the dependent is unmarried, has no dependents, lives in New Jersey or is a full-time student, and has no other coverage. Age 26 is the federal ACA rule, which New Jersey extends.

question: An insured's group health policy covers dependents. Coverage for the insured's newborn child begins:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:27-30 requires benefits for a newborn from the moment of birth, including care of congenital defects. If an added premium is due, the policy may require notice and payment within 90 days to continue coverage.

question: After an illness, a sales manager returns to her job full time, but her income is 40% lower. Which benefit pays part of her lost income?
explanation: Residual disability benefits pay in proportion to the loss of income when the insured can still work but earns less. She is not totally disabled under either an own-occupation or any-occupation definition, and presumptive disability requires a severe loss such as sight, speech, hearing or two limbs.

question: A dentist who owns her practice becomes disabled. Which coverage pays her office rent, utilities and staff salaries, but not her own income?
explanation: Business overhead expense coverage reimburses the ongoing costs of running the business while the owner is disabled, but never the owner's salary. Its premiums are deductible as a business expense, so the benefits are taxable.

question: A tech company wants funds to replace lost profits and recruit help if its lead engineer becomes disabled. The company should buy:
explanation: Key person disability coverage is owned by and pays the business to offset losses when a vital employee is disabled. Disability buy-sell coverage instead funds the purchase of a disabled owner's share, usually after a long elimination period of 1 to 2 years.

question: A young physician wants the right to buy more disability coverage as her income grows, without new proof of insurability. She needs a:
explanation: The future increase option lets the insured add coverage at set dates or income levels without evidence of insurability. A Social Security rider instead pays an extra benefit when Social Security disability benefits are denied, and a cost-of-living rider adjusts benefits during a claim.

question: Hank suffers a fatal heart attack while driving, and his car then hits a tree. His accidental death and dismemberment policy will:
optionA: Pay the principal sum for accidental death
optionB: Pay the capital sum of half the principal
optionC: Pay nothing, since illness caused death
optionD: Pay twice the principal sum for the crash
explanation: AD&D is accident-only coverage that pays only when an accident is the direct cause of death or dismemberment. The heart attack, a sickness, caused his death, so the later crash does not trigger the principal sum.

question: A family wants protection against catastrophic bills, with high limits, a deductible and coinsurance, rather than low-limit first-dollar coverage. They should buy:
explanation: Major medical coverage pays a broad range of expenses with high limits after a deductible, with coinsurance sharing costs. Basic hospital, surgical and medical plans pay first-dollar benefits but have low limits for each type of service.

question: Lisa's major medical plan has a $1,000 deductible and 80/20 coinsurance. She incurs $6,000 in covered charges. How much does Lisa pay?
explanation: Lisa pays the $1,000 deductible plus 20% of the remaining $5,000, which is $1,000, for a total of $2,000. Applying 20% to the full $6,000 on top of the deductible gives the wrong $2,200.

question: A new retiree wants a private plan that replaces Original Medicare Parts A and B and often includes drug coverage. She should choose:
optionA: Medicare Part D prescription drug coverage
optionC: A Medicare supplement Plan G policy
explanation: Medicare Advantage (Part C) plans are offered by private insurers in place of Parts A and B, often bundling Part D drug coverage. Part D covers only prescription drugs, and Medigap supplements Original Medicare rather than replacing it.

question: Two insurers both sell Medicare supplement Plan G, at different premiums. How do the benefits of the two policies compare?
optionB: The costlier plan has more benefits
optionC: They differ by insurer and state
optionD: Each insurer sets its own Plan G benefits
explanation: Medigap plans are standardized, so a given letter has the same benefits from every insurer, and every plan includes the Plan A core benefits. Shoppers compare price and service, and a Medicare SELECT version uses a provider network in exchange for a lower premium.

question: Helen's assets exceed her state's Medicaid limit, so she pays her own nursing home bills until her assets fall below it. This process is called:
explanation: Medicaid is a needs-based program run by the states with federal funding, and spend-down is how applicants reduce assets or income to qualify. The 5-year look-back period instead reviews earlier asset transfers made to qualify.

question: Grace can still eat and use the toilet, but she now needs help bathing and dressing for the foreseeable future. Under a tax-qualified LTC policy, she:
optionA: Needs to lose 3 ADLs to qualify
optionB: Must first be hospitalized for 3 days
explanation: Tax-qualified LTC benefits begin when the insured cannot perform 2 of the 6 ADLs (bathing, dressing, eating, toileting, transferring, continence) for an expected 90 days or more, or has a severe cognitive impairment. Prior hospitalization cannot be required.

question: A buyer of a New Jersey Medicare supplement policy may return it for a full premium refund within:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:26A-8 requires a notice on the first page that the applicant may return the policy within 30 days of delivery for a premium refund if not satisfied for any reason.

question: Under N.J.S.A. 17B:26A-4, a Medicare supplement policy may not deny a preexisting condition claim for losses incurred more than how long after coverage begins?
explanation: The statute bars denying claims for losses more than six months after the effective date for a preexisting condition, and limits the definition to conditions treated or advised within six months before coverage.

question: New Jersey's small employer health benefits law applies to employers that averaged no more than how many eligible employees in the prior year?
explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:27A-17 defines a small employer as one with an average of at least two but not more than 50 eligible employees, most of them employed in New Jersey. Larger groups buy coverage outside the small employer program.

question: Under the New Jersey Temporary Disability Benefits Law, benefits for any one period of a worker's own disability are limited to:
explanation: N.J.S.A. 43:21-39(b)(1) bars payment for more than 26 weeks in one period of the worker's own disability. Twelve weeks is the cap for family temporary disability leave.

question: A worker's own disability under the state TDB plan lasts four weeks. The first seven days of that disability are:
optionA: Never paid, as a waiting period
optionB: Paid only if she was hospitalized
optionC: Paid, as benefits ran three weeks
explanation: N.J.S.A. 43:21-39(a)(1) sets a seven-day waiting period but pays those days retroactively once benefits have been payable for three consecutive weeks. Workers compensation covers only work-related injuries.
